topics.topic: Allocation and stability of the global store record order
questions: What durable global position orders records across all model types, when is it allocated, and does updating a mutable entity preserve its original position or receive another one?
What is the total store order within a transaction that creates multiple records, and does a later status change retain the record's original position?
Is the store order assigned only when a record is created, or also on each transition or update, and is a record's position permanently stable?

quotes: record_change: [DETERMINISM_OR_ORDERING] Every record written gets one store position from next_store_position, a single strictly increasing counter shared by all record types, called inside the transaction that writes the record; store order is the order of these positions, every collection the module returns is in store order unless the function says otherwise, and Activation and FlowActivation records are identified by their store_position.

record_change: [DETERMINISM_OR_ORDERING] The records one change writes take their store positions with every StoredValue first, in the order the variant names them, then the other records in the order the field-assignment note of its variant lists them, the elements of a list of records in list order (a RecordRunProgressChange's executions in (node_id, map_index) order); an update keeps the record's position, so positions never depend on record type or database insertion order.

next_store_position: [BEHAVIOR] MUST read the counter row with load_store_position_counter for = models.StoreCounterName store_position, take one more than its last_position, or 1 when no counter row exists yet, write that number back as last_position with upsert_store_position_counter on the same repository, and return it; it is called only by this module inside the transaction of a change, so a change that fails leaves the counter as it was and no two records ever share a position.
judgement.why: State 7 defines allocation, within-change ordering, global monotonicity, and position preservation on lifecycle updates.

topics.topic: Filesystem ownership, type, permissions, ACL, and hard-link requirements for private store data
questions: What exact ownership, permission-bit and file-type conditions make the data directory and each entry “private”, especially for directories versus regular files?
What exact ownership, permission and file-type conditions make the data directory and each contained object "private," and are hard-linked files allowed?
What exact owner, group, mode-bit, ACL, and other-access conditions define “private” for the data directory and each kind of entry?

judgement.why: This is the same unchanged data-directory privacy question already judged in P1, and the reopening change did not alter that rule.

precedent.topic: Data-directory privacy, allowed object types, and continued integrity enforcement
quotes: The directory and everything in it are private to the kernel's user; the kernel refuses to start otherwise.
precedent.why: The topic concerns A18's unchanged data-directory privacy rule, and the Linux/O_NOFOLLOW change to A17 and A20 did not make that existing question matter.

topics.topic: Observable event that serializes concurrent surface requests
questions: What event fixes the total order of concurrent incoming requests?
Which observable event determines the order of two concurrently received requests?
What observable event fixes the total order of concurrent requests: receipt of the first byte, completion of message parsing, enqueueing after validation, or transport-provided order?

judgement.why: This is the same concurrent-request arrival-order question already judged in P2, on unchanged text.

precedent.topic: Event defining serialized arrival order for concurrent requests
quotes:
Surface requests are handled one at a time in the order they arrive: one request, including the run
   advancement it causes (A13), ends before the next begins, so an approval, a
   cancellation and a resume of one run never race.
precedent.why: The serialization sentence is unchanged, and the reopening change did not affect concurrent-request ordering.

topics.topic: Startup behavior when cleanup targets cannot be inspected or removed
questions: What happens when a temporary file or unreferenced content file cannot be inspected or removed during startup cleanup?
For each startup-cleanup target, does removal failure stop startup or leave the object for a later start, and which rule wins when the cause also violates a startup security check?
What happens when a temporary file or unreferenced value byte cannot be inspected or removed during startup cleanup?

judgement.why: This is the same startup-cleanup failure question already judged in P5, and the reopening change did not affect cleanup.

precedent.topic: Startup behavior when temporary or unreferenced-object cleanup fails
quotes:
On start, temporary files,
   value bytes no record names (left by a failed call, K-10; owner,
   2026-10-07) and
   the spool directories of runs that ended and do not keep their spool (A14) are
   removed; nothing else is. A spool directory that cannot be removed does not
   stop the start: it stays, never served, until a later start removes it.
precedent.why: The cleanup passage is unchanged, and the reopening change did not affect cleanup failures.

topics.topic: Symlink and relative-path rules for traversing the data-directory path and store paths
questions: May `data_directory` itself or one of its path ancestors be a symbolic link, and what component-walk rule applies when opening store paths?
May the configured data-directory path or one of its ancestor components be a symbolic link, and from where is a relative data-directory path walked?
Must the data-directory path and every directory component beneath it also be opened without following symbolic links, or is only each final file protected?

judgement.why: This is the same store-path symlink traversal question already judged in P10; the change concerns configuration and credential paths, not A18's store rule.

precedent.topic: Symlink-safe component traversal and protection against path-replacement races
quotes:
Every
   file of the directory is opened without following symbolic links; a link
   found at start stops the start, and one found later makes that store call
   fail with nothing written.
precedent.why: A18's store traversal requirement is unchanged; making A17's separate configuration traversal more explicit did not alter the store rule.

topics.topic: Which store structures startup creates and which must already exist
questions: Which missing store objects are created on first start, and which missing objects make startup fail?
Does startup create a missing data directory, database, value area, fixture area and spool area, or must an installer create some or all of them beforehand?
On first start, which missing directory, database, value area, fixture area, and spool structures does the kernel create, and which missing structures make startup fail?

judgement.why: This is the same first-start store-layout provisioning question already judged in P4, on unchanged A18 text.

precedent.topic: Provisioning and handling of a partially existing data-directory layout
quotes:
The data directory holds one SQLite database with every kernel record, a
   content-addressed area of value bytes and file fixtures named by digest, and
   the run spool, one subdirectory per run.
precedent.why: The required layout passage is unchanged, and the Linux/O_NOFOLLOW change did not make provisioning behavior newly material.

topics.topic: Detection and handling of missing, corrupted, colliding, or otherwise damaged stored content
questions: When startup, reuse or a read encounters a database-referenced value or fixture file that is missing or does not match its recorded digest and size, must startup fail, must the individual store call fail, or may the file be trusted by name?
How does the store handle a digest collision or corrupted existing object at a content-addressed path?
Which store-integrity failures refuse startup, which produce `internal_error` and stop the kernel, and whether any may be repaired automatically?

quotes: put_value_bytes: [PATH_OR_ARTIFACT_POLICY] MUST store the bytes in the content-addressed area under their digest: when a file for that digest already exists it returns without writing; otherwise it writes a temporary file in the same area, flushes and fsyncs it, re-checks its digest and size, and renames it into place without overwriting, so a crash leaves either no file or the complete file and a completed file is never rewritten.

read_value_bytes: [VALIDATION_ERROR] MUST raise UnknownReferenceError when the identity names no record, and StoreInternalError when the bytes of an existing record are missing, unreadable, reached through a symbolic link, or differ from the record's digest or size.

run_start_sequence: [VALIDATION_ERROR] Every step is required: the first step that raises — InstallationRejectedError, RefusedError from the instance check, a store refusal, SandboxUnavailableError, StopRequiredError or any other exception — stops the sequence there and propagates unchanged to the caller, the same exception with its own reason; before it propagates MUST write the failing step's name — load_installation, check_installed_instances, open_store, probe_sandbox, recover_in_flight_attempts or recover_running_runs — as one line to standard error, so the step is named there and the reason stays the exception's own; no later step runs and nothing is retried or skipped.
judgement.why: State 7 specifies reuse of an existing digest path, validation on reads, the resulting internal error, and startup failure propagation.

topics.topic: Ordering and failure precedence of startup validation, locking, cleanup, and sandbox checks
questions: In what order are A18's startup actions performed, and which failure is reported when several conditions fail?

When several startup conditions fail, which A18 failure is reported first, and at what point relative to configuration validation and the sandbox probe is the data-directory lock acquired and cleanup performed?

quotes: run_start_sequence: [ORCHESTRATION] MUST call, in exactly this order and each exactly once: load_installation with config_path; check_installed_instances with the loaded Installation; open_store with that Installation's data_directory; probe_sandbox; recover_in_flight_attempts; recover_running_runs (A03 rule 8, A09 rule 1, A14 rule 5, A18).

open_store: [BEHAVIOR] MUST run, in this order, stopping at the first failure: take an exclusive non-blocking lock on data_directory itself, opened as a directory without following links and held for the life of the process, so the lock creates no file; check that data_directory and everything inside it are owned by the process's effective user and grant no permission to group or others; walk the directory without following links and find no symbolic link; then open the database file inside data_directory as the module's one SQLite connection with synchronous FULL, after os.lstat finds that path no symbolic link; create its tables with create_store_schema, which leaves existing tables as they are; then remove the module's own temporary files left by an interrupted publish and every file of the content-addressed area whose digest no StoredValue names — a trial case's file fixture is itself a StoredValue of file carriage (M21), so no other record names a value file —, which is a digest for which list_stored_value_rows_by_value_digest answers no row, and create the content-addressed area and the spool area when absent.
judgement.why: State 7 fixes both the overall startup sequence and the complete first-failure order inside store opening.

topics.topic: Publication, verification, reuse, and orphan-cleanup guarantees for trial fixtures
questions: Are trial file fixtures subject to the same flush, digest-and-size verification, atomic rename, non-overwrite and equal-byte reuse rules, and how are orphan fixtures from a failed store call cleaned up?
Do trial file fixtures receive the same temporary-write, digest verification, atomic publication, no-overwrite, and orphan-cleanup guarantees, and if not, what guarantees apply?

quotes:
`module:store`. Publish value bytes or a file fixture complete and digest-checked into the
content-addressed area, equal bytes once.

Written to a temporary file, flushed, checked, renamed; a completed file is
never overwritten; equal bytes are stored once (A18 rule 4).

judgement.why: The later store API explicitly applies atomic digest-checked publication, reuse, durability, and orphan cleanup to file fixtures.

topics.topic: Secure configuration and credential path component-walk rules
questions: Which lexical path components are accepted, rejected or traversed during the component-by-component walk?
How must intermediate components and the final component be opened, including whether intermediates require `O_DIRECTORY` and whether search-only directories must work through `O_PATH`?
What exact component sequence is walked for those path forms, and which forms are refused rather than normalized or traversed?

quotes:
Here and in rule 2 the path is opened component by component without
   following a symbolic link at any of them, each component with Linux's
   `O_NOFOLLOW`, whose presence no code tests (A20 rule 3) — the path as
   given, an absolute one walked from the root directory and a relative one
   from the working directory, and a component that cannot be opened so, for
   whatever reason, making the file one that cannot be read —, and the checks and the read use
   that one opened file, so the file checked is the file read.

A release runs on Linux and
   on no other host, no version named (owner, 2026-10-18). Another system, or
   a Linux without `O_NOFOLLOW`, is unsupported: the kernel neither tests for
   it nor defines what it does there; the sandbox's facilities stay A03's,
   which the start probes.
judgement.divergence: One careful implementation rejects paths containing empty, repeated-separator, `.`, `..`, or trailing-separator components and opens intermediates only as directories; another traverses or normalizes those forms using different open flags. The installer notices because the same configuration or credential path is accepted by one kernel and refused by the other.
judgement.why: The new component-walk rule fixes the starting directory and `O_NOFOLLOW` but leaves behaviorally observable lexical-component and intermediate-open choices unspecified.
